generic_points: Homeowners are primarily concerned about high upfront costs and look for subsidies such as the BEG/KfW grants to make heat pumps affordable.
Many worry about whether a heat pump works efficiently in older, poorly insulated buildings without extensive renovation.
Running costs and electricity prices versus gas and oil are a central decision factor, with interest in heat pump tariffs and combining with photovoltaics.
The Gebäudeenergiegesetz (the so-called Heizungsgesetz) creates uncertainty and confusion about legal obligations and deadlines.
Finding a reliable installer is difficult due to long waiting times, skilled-labor shortages and mixed quality of offers.
Noise from outdoor units and neighbor disputes or placement rules are a common concern.
Trust is built through independent advice from energy consultants, consumer advocates (Verbraucherzentrale), and peer reviews from other owners.
Information is sought via Google, YouTube, comparison portals, forums, and manufacturer websites; Facebook groups and Reddit also play a role.
Brands such as Viessmann, Vaillant, Stiebel Eltron, Bosch and Daikin dominate the conversation, with a focus on German quality and reliability.
Common messages that resonate are independence from fossil fuels, climate protection, future-proofing, and increasing property value.
Existing users report on efficiency (COP/JAZ), hydraulic balancing, flow temperature and setting optimizations, and sometimes disappointment with higher-than-expected bills.
Political debate, media skepticism and misinformation about heat pumps shape sentiment, with a mix of enthusiasm and distrust among older homeowners.

for_goals.headline: The audience is practical and sceptical: they swap experiences in Facebook groups and YouTube comments, and their sharpest tensions are the old-radiator flow temperature and the cost of maintenance that keeps the warranty alive.
for_goals.success_measure: Peers answer with their own maintenance positions, flow temperatures and JAZ values in the replies, so you can see which tension draws the most detail.

creative_brief.objective: Understand the audience: learn which tensions, objections and numbers German WP owners and shoppers care about, by joining their conversations with concrete, comparable content.
creative_brief.audience: German homeowners (about 40-70) in single-family houses and older buildings who are weighing a WP in place of gas or oil, are at the quote stage, or already live with one. They are practical and sceptical, and trust peer reports more than manufacturers.
creative_brief.insight: Owners don't doubt the WP itself. They doubt that they can see what they pay for and what they get: maintenance without breakdown, quotes without a clear Leistungsumfang, and efficiency promised without winter context or the limits of the old radiators.
creative_brief.message: Show the positions and the real numbers, in the Altbau too.
creative_brief.tone: Practical, direct and sceptical, peer to peer. Measured and numerical where results are shared. Blunt is fine, brochure language is not. Rare emoji.

objection_handling.response: Verständlich: Wenn auf dem Angebot nur ein Preis steht, kann keiner prüfen, was der Heizungsmonteur macht. Frag nach den Positionen der Wartung nach Herstellervorschrift und vergleiche, ob Regiewartung nach Aufwand oder feste Positionen angesetzt sind. Ob die Garantie die Kosten wert ist, solltest du mit der Aufstellung rechnen. Adapt to your offer: list what your maintenance covers, position by position, and say how it relates to the warranty terms, or state clearly that you don't offer maintenance.

Im Altbau ist das mehr als ein Gerätetausch: Die Heizflächen und die Vorlauftemperatur entscheiden mit, wie effizient die WP läuft. Ich verspreche nicht, dass alte Heizkörper reichen. Erst prüfen, was nötig ist, dann entscheiden. Adapt to your offer: say whether you check radiators and flow temperature before quoting, and how that appears in your quote.

Lass dir keine WP aufschwatzen, die falsch ausgelegt ist oder nicht zum Haus passt. Frag, wie Größe und Heizkörper geprüft wurden, und hol ein zweites Angebot ein. Adapt to your offer: describe how you size a unit and which house data you ask for, so buyers can check it.

Ein SCOP aus dem Prospekt sagt nichts über schlechte Winterwerte. Aussagekräftiger ist eine gemessene JAZ mit Marke, Jahren und der Angabe, ob Warmwasser dabei ist. Gute Werte aus dem Alltag sind wertvoll, schlechte auch. Adapt to your offer: publish measured values with context next to the data-sheet figure, including winter, or point to independent owner reports.

Wartungsangebot nach einem Jahr: Pauschale würde ich nicht mehr akzeptieren. Ich will die Positionen sehen.

So sieht ein Angebot aus, das uns vorliegt:
🔧 Gerät: Bosch AW 5 OR-S + CS5800 iAW 12 MB
🔧 Angeboten wird eine „Regiewartung“ (Wartung nach Zeit und Aufwand), abgerechnet als Pauschale
🔧 Preis: netto 377 €
🔧 Aufschlüsselung der Positionen: keine

Da fragt man sich: Was genau macht der Heizungsmonteur für das Geld?

Wir hören immer wieder, dass Wartung für das, was gemacht wird, zu teuer wirkt. Das ist unser Eindruck aus den Beiträgen, keine Tatsache. Einer schreibt, man solle darauf achten, dass nach Herstellervorschrift gewartet und jeder Punkt im Wartungsprotokoll abgearbeitet wird. Andere fragen sich, ob die Garantie die jährlichen Kosten wert ist, wenn man z. B. Magnet- und Schlammabscheider ohnehin selbst reinigt.

Unsere Fragen an euch:
➡️ Welche Positionen stehen in eurem Angebot?
➡️ Welche davon hält ihr nach Herstellervorschrift für nötig?
➡️ Ist euch die Garantie die Wartung wert?

Wir sammeln eure Antworten und machen daraus eine Checkliste der Positionen, die ihr beim Vergleichen nutzen könnt.

Schreibt uns in die Kommentare, was in eurem Wartungsangebot steht und was ihr dafür zahlt.

[Szene: Heizkörper im Altbau, Thermometer am Vorlauf]
Achtung, Altbau: Alte Heizkörper können deine WP ausbremsen. So habe ich nachgemessen.

In den Beiträgen heißt es: 60 °C Vorlauftemperatur sind für eine effiziente WP zu hoch, 35 bis 45 °C wären besser. Alte Heizkörper treiben sie hoch, weil ihre Fläche oft zu klein ist.

Nur das Gerät tauschen reicht nicht. Die Heizflächen richtig hinzubekommen ist die größere Baustelle. Manche waren nach dem ersten Winter ernüchtert.

[Szene: Heizkennlinie am Display]
Vorlauftemperatur an kalten Tagen, Heizkennlinie, Räume, die nicht warm werden. Eine Heizlastberechnung klärt, was nötig ist. Manchen half schon der Tausch einzelner großer Heizkörper.

Wie sieht es bei dir aus? Schreib deine Vorlauftemperatur und deine Heizkörper in die Kommentare.

hypotheses.statement: German homeowners' main barrier to a heat pump is total cost and uncertainty about the KfW/BEG subsidy, not the technology itself.
hypotheses.why: Posts criticise expensive quotes and maintenance, and one mentions KfW conditions, but there is no evidence on subsidy uncertainty as the main barrier.

hypotheses.statement: Many homeowners in older, unrenovated buildings doubt that a heat pump works efficiently without full insulation or underfloor heating, and trust peer experience reports more than manufacturers.
hypotheses.why: Old radiators and cast-iron radiators are named as the efficiency problem, and posters distrust advertised figures and installer promises while citing their own numbers. Insulation is not covered in these posts.

hypotheses.statement: Political debate around the Gebäudeenergiegesetz (Heizungsgesetz) has created distrust and wait-and-see behaviour, with many delaying decisions.
hypotheses.why: No cited post discusses the GEG or Heizungsgesetz or wait-and-see behaviour.

hypotheses.statement: Installer availability, long waits and inconsistent quotes are major frustrations, and owners rely on forum advice to judge installers and sizing.
hypotheses.why: Posters ask for installer recommendations, report an unresponsive installer and criticise unclear quotes, and forum replies advise on radiators and sizing. Long waits are not shown.

hypotheses.statement: Existing owners worry about noise (Außeneinheit), real-life JAZ/electricity costs and winter performance, and these concerns shape the views of prospective buyers.
hypotheses.why: Posts raise noise comparisons, JAZ and SCOP values, and disappointment after the first winter. Their effect on prospective buyers is only partly visible.

Important notice upfront. Of course, the electricity must be prepared or connected by an electrician. Safety always comes first when connecting to the grid. In this video I take you along on my big adventure installing an air-water heat pump myself. I show you my device and my system in the garden and tell you honestly and unvarnished how I implemented the entire project on my own, what hurdles there were, and how my system works after now twenty years of wood stove experience. To avoid any trouble, I've taped over the logo and model designation on the heat pump for the video. Here's what to expect in the video. First. The backstory and my motivation. I tell you why after installing my solar panels, which I show you in the video, I absolutely wanted a heat pump and why a simple immersion heater in a water tank was not an option for me. My solar system has a proud ten kilowatts peak capacity. Second. The rock-solid foundation. I tell you how I saved myself from pouring a concrete slab. You learn how I dug out the earth, packed it with stones and water, and placed an old thick concrete block with twenty centimetres overhang on top. Third. The pipes and insulation. Why I chose thick, weatherproof rubber insulation and flexible white PE pipes. I also tell you how I laid the lines ten metres through under the floorboards to the water tank. Fourth. The honest noise check. I show you the heat pump outside in the garden and tell you how loud the device really is and why the control panel directly on my bedroom wall doesn't disturb my sleep at night at all. Fifth. The technology and safety components. I explain why the passive pressure of my old system wasn't enough for the heat pump. You learn all about installing the additional pump, the check valve, the strainer, the dirt separator and the filter. Sixth. Why the self-installation is legal. I explain why the factory-sealed monoblock system of the heat pump means that you as a DIYer can legally lay the pipes yourself. Seventh. The weak points of the cheap heat pump. I haven't opened the device for the video, but I tell you exactly what's hidden inside. We talk about the missing partition wall between the heat chamber and the fan and about the unprotected pipe bends, which pose a real frost risk. I reveal my safety rule with the heating pump on level one in frost conditions. Eighth. The winter reality check and the roof. I show you the roof I built for my heat pump and explain why that's important in snow. I also show you in a photo the dirt from just one year on the fins. You learn why cleaning in autumn is mandatory and why the cooling fins freeze starting at plus six degrees because of the air humidity. Ninth. My honest assessment in summer and winter. I tell you how the eight-hundred-litre water tank is heated and the heat lasts through the whole night. But I also tell you the truth about rainy summer days and why the solar system brings almost nothing in the four hard winter months of November, December, January and February. Hi [name],

I can well understand your experience. I'm a real estate agent and see this problem frequently in old buildings. 60°C flow temperature is definitely too high for efficient heat pump use. Optimal would be 35-45°C.

The problem usually lies in the insufficient heating surface of the old radiators. They are designed for high flow temperatures, but heat pumps work best with low temperatures. You have two sensible options:

1. Larger/additional radiators - relatively inexpensive effort, immediately feasible
2. Surface heating (floor/wall) – more expensive but the best long-term solution

For old buildings I would start with larger radiators first. Look for low-temperature radiators with more heating surface. That often already brings significant improvement without a major construction site.

evidence.text_en: Baffled and angry: I frequently receive heat pump quotes for review and often think: "wow, how can someone send that out." My findings: - Customers are sometimes really sold for a fool - Positions missing, subsidies endangered --> recently experienced again, KfW makes no exceptions! The subsidy conditions must be met. - Heat pump incorrectly dimensioned (way too expensive hardware, high operating costs through heating rod, wear through short-cycling) - Offers are outrageously overpriced. Due to the recent change in subsidies, the topic has become even more complex again. But one shouldn't have to read in forums for weeks with other half-experts until you're sure and can buy in good conscience. A heat pump is currently the most complex purchase you can make. Technology, subsidies, 30 line items. We are now decisively taking action against this. This check creates transparency. Here you really compare apples with apples! PS: Our motivation is the heating transition. This can only work if there is high acceptance and penetration of renewable heating. 134,000 gas heaters were still installed in H1 this year. Also because the heat pump offers are too complex / time-consuming and overpriced. The individual installer doesn't care. We do!
